children.text: Quezon City's signature park centers on the 66m shrine where Commonwealth President Manuel L. Quezon and his wife are laid to rest. With four free museums, wooded paths, bike rentals, an elevated promenade and a food park, it combines history and relaxation in a half-day visit.
Quezon Memorial Circle is a park of about 25–27 hectares in the heart of Quezon City, in the northeast of Metro Manila, ringed by the Elliptical Road loop. At its center stands a

shrine honoring Manuel L. Quezon, president of the Philippine Commonwealth and founder of Quezon City, and beneath it rest President Quezon and his wife, Aurora. It is Quezon City's favorite place to unwind, where crowds come every day to walk and exercise, and a historic site where you can trace modern Philippine history in one place.
The site was originally chosen for a national capitol, whose cornerstone was laid in
, but construction stopped because of World War II. After President Quezon died in exile in the United States in
, a memorial project began; architect Federico Ilustre won the
design competition, and construction started in
. The shrine was completed in
, and Quezon's remains were moved here from the Manila North Cemetery in
. Quezon City was the capital of the Philippines from
, and this park was planned as the heart of that new capital.
The shrine's three pylons join into one, symbolizing the three island groups of Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao, and its

height is said to honor Quezon's death in his 66th year. At the top stand three mourning angels by Italian sculptor Francesco Riccardo Monti, holding wreaths of sampaguita, the national flower. The base houses the Quezon museum run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) and the tomb of the presidential couple, and the shrine has been declared a National Cultural Treasure.
Today the park is much more than a historic site. Under the city's redevelopment program, an elevated promenade linking it to the neighboring Ninoy Aquino Parks and Wildlife Center opened in
November 2025
, and in

a skate park, tennis courts, a dog park and a multipurpose lawn of about 12,000㎡ opened one after another. Entry to the park is free, as are most of the museums, so it suits history lovers, families with children and long-stay visitors looking for green space in the city alike.

blocks.title: Quezon Memorial Shrine and its angels

children.text: The shrine's three white marble pylons rise in the middle of the park. From the plaza in front you can see the angel sculptures at the top together with the reliefs of Philippine history on the lower walls, and on one side of the plaza stands a statue of Quezon delivering a speech.

A free museum on the shrine's lower level, with five galleries covering Quezon's life from childhood through the independence movement to the Commonwealth years. There is also a hologram recreating his inaugural address and a special exhibit on Doña Aurora. It is open Tuesday to Sunday,
In the round hall at the center of the museum lies President Quezon's black marble sarcophagus, and beside it is the tomb of Doña Aurora, moved here in
. It is a solemn place, so keep your voice down and follow the guidance on photography.
The house on Gilmore Street in New Manila, where the Quezon family lived from
, was moved to the park and restored in

. Its airy layout, built for Quezon while he suffered from tuberculosis, and period furniture remain, and the Philippine Red Cross was founded in its living room. It has sometimes operated by appointment, so check ahead.
A free museum opened in

, displaying official cars used by Philippine presidents during their terms, restored to their original condition. Seeing presidential cars from different eras side by side is a particular hit with children. It is closed on Mondays.
The newest museum, opened in
. Using materials and household items from the Aquino family home on Times Street, it recreates the living room, kitchen and bedrooms of a middle-class Filipino home of the
. It is open free of charge from Tuesday to Sunday.
On Saturdays you can rent bamboo bikes (Bambike) behind the Quezon Heritage House for about
per hour and ride around the park. The elevated promenade over Elliptical Road has a bike ramp that makes it easy for strollers and wheelchairs too, and it lights up in the evening.

blocks.title: Peace bell, gardens and food park

children.text: The World Peace Bell installed in
, a flower garden, children's playgrounds and the Circle of Fun amusement park are scattered along the wooded paths. When you get hungry, take a break with street food at the QMC Food Park.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Focus on the shrine and museums

children.text: Get off at MRT Line 3 Quezon Avenue Station and take a jeepney or Grab to the park. It takes about
10–15 minutes
As the museum opens, enter the Quezon museum beneath the shrine to see its five galleries and the tomb of the presidential couple.
Look at the angel sculptures and history reliefs from the shrine plaza, take photos, then walk to the Presidential Car Museum.
Choose either the Quezon Heritage House or Bahay Modernismo. Check the heritage house's visiting arrangements in advance.
Have lunch at the restaurant row near the park's east entrance.
Pass the World Peace Bell and the flower garden, then finish with a walk along the wooded paths.
Most museums are closed on Mondays, so plan this route for Tuesday to Sunday. On a Monday, switch to walking in the park, the elevated promenade and the restaurants.
Cross the elevated promenade to explore the Ninoy Aquino Parks and Wildlife Center. It closes at
Rent a bamboo bike behind the Quezon Heritage House and ride slowly around the park loop.
Check out the new lawn and skate park, and photograph the shrine's silhouette at sunset.
Move to Maginhawa Street east of the park for dinner at its cafés and restaurants. It is about a
15–20-minute
walk.
Take one more look at the illuminated shrine and head back to your hotel by Grab.
Bike rentals currently run only on Saturdays. On other days, walk or jog instead, and since the park closes at
, don't stay too late.
Quezon Avenue Station on MRT Line 3, which runs along EDSA, is the closest. It takes about
25–30 minutes
from Ayala Station in Makati, and with the 50% discount in place since
March 2026
, the fare is about
. The discount is a temporary measure with no set end date, so check the latest announcements.
Quezon Avenue Station is about
1.5km
from the park:
20–25 minutes
on foot along Quezon Avenue, or around
10 minutes
by jeepney or Grab. North Avenue Station is a similar distance away.
MRT Line 7's Quezon Memorial Circle Station is under construction right next to the park, with opening targeted for
Jeepneys marked "Philcoa" on the windshield run straight from Ermita (TM Kalaw) and Quiapo along Quezon Avenue to the side of the park. The ride takes
40 minutes–1 hour 20 minutes
depending on traffic, and the minimum fare is about
You can also catch the same "Philcoa" jeepney in front of MRT Quezon Avenue Station and get off on Elliptical Road. Tell the driver beforehand to drop you at "Quezon Memorial Circle" or "City Hall."
Route 1 of the free city bus run by Quezon City (Q City Bus) runs between Cubao and Quezon City Hall and stops on Elliptical Road. Buses come about every
1 hour
(about every
30 minutes
at rush hour), and routes and schedules are adjusted often, so check City Hall announcements.
You can also take the EDSA Carousel bus along the EDSA busway, get off at the Quezon Avenue stop and transfer to a jeepney.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) it is about
22km
, taking
45 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
depending on traffic, and a Grab costs about
. Fares go up at rush hour and on rainy days.

Enter "Quezon Memorial Circle" as your destination, but choose "Quezon Memorial Shrine" if you plan to start with the museum, or the East Avenue entrance if you're heading for the restaurants first, to save walking. If you drive, the park's parking costs about
per car per day.

Elliptical Road, which rings the park, is a large loop where cars move fast, so jaywalking is very dangerous. Use the underpass linked to Quezon City Hall, the underpass on the Philcoa (Commonwealth Avenue) side, or the elevated promenade from the Ninoy Aquino park to get in.
December–February
is the most pleasant time. Mornings and evenings are relatively cool, so you can walk the wooded paths for a long time without strain.
March–May
brings little rain, but midday temperatures climb close to
, so put the museums in the middle of the day and save park walks for early morning or after
June–November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and in
July–September

passing typhoons sometimes close parts of the park temporarily. On rainy days, focus on the indoor museums. The park is busiest on weekend mornings with locals walking, jogging and doing Zumba, and quietest on weekday mornings.
August 19
, President Quezon's birthday, is a commemorative day in Quezon City, and ceremonies are often held at the shrine. At year's end the park is decorated with lights, and on the night of
December 31
the city government's New Year countdown draws huge crowds.

If you're only coming for the park, you can stay in Makati, BGC or central Manila and visit on a half-day trip. If you'd like to stay in Quezon City, there are plenty of business and mid-range hotels around Vertis North and Eton Centris between MRT North Avenue and Quezon Avenue stations, and around Araneta City in Cubao with its shopping malls, at about
a night. The park is about
10–25 minutes
away by Grab.

Near the park's east entrance is a cluster of restaurants and cafés, including long-established Filipino chains such as The Aristocrat, Max's Restaurant and Bacolod Chicken Inasal, good for Filipino home-style dishes like chicken inasal, sinigang and pancit. At the QMC Food Park and the stalls you can enjoy barbecue skewers, halo-halo and fresh fruit shakes cheaply. In the evening, head to Maginhawa Street east of the park, Quezon City's best-known food street, lined with small restaurants and cafés popular with UP Diliman students.
Most museums open Tuesday to Sunday around
and close on Mondays. Closing times vary slightly by venue, so arrive at least
1 hour
before closing.
The park is open
, and many locals are already jogging before sunrise. Early morning, when there are fewer people, is best for photos.
The shrine plaza has almost no shade. Bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and escape the midday heat inside the museums.

Bike rentals run only on Saturdays and there are few bikes, so you may have to wait in the afternoon. Free guided bike tours for the first visitors to sign up are sometimes held on the first and third Saturdays of the month, so check the latest announcements.
The park works to reduce single-use plastic, so bringing a reusable bottle is handy. Always put trash in the designated bins.
The Quezon Heritage House has operated by appointment at times. If you really want to see it, ask the Quezon City tourism office or the park administration office in advance.
When booking a Grab, decide on the exit (City Hall side, Philcoa side or East Avenue side) so you don't miss your driver.
If you want to prepare for the shrine and museum, read a little about the
period, when Quezon led the Commonwealth and prepared the Philippines for independence, and the exhibits will make much more sense.

Ongoing city redevelopment and construction of the MRT Line 7 station mean some paths and facilities at Quezon Memorial Circle may be temporarily closed or relocated. The dancing fountain mentioned in older guides was removed during redevelopment in
. Check the latest Quezon City Hall announcements before you go.
Never jaywalk across Elliptical Road; always use the underpasses or the elevated promenade.
Crowds are huge on weekends, holidays and year-end events. Watch out for pickpockets and keep your phone and wallet in front of you.
Access to the elevated promenade is free. In
February 2026
a security guard tried to collect money and the city government stepped in, so don't pay if anyone asks for a fee.
Avoid food and loud voices inside the tomb and museums, and follow each gallery's photography rules.
In the rainy season the wooded paths and lawns get muddy and there are many mosquitoes. Bring sneakers and insect repellent.
